A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same persona inference and persona tailoring work. All 23 pages in each version, including figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A.1–A.12, support comparison. Relocated main-text and appendix results can be matched.

before.justification: V1 reports original persona-inference experiments, personalization comparisons, ablations, and human evaluations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and reports revised human evaluations and additional annotator-agreement results.

M1.justification: The PI/PT pipeline, LLaMA-405B persona generation, LLaMA-8B tailoring, and few-shot, SFT, and DPO procedures remain unchanged. The added persona-format description and rewritten DPO explanation document the existing method rather than establish a procedural change.

E1.justification: Benchmark coverage remains BeaverTails, SHP, Anthropic HHH, and Mnemonic, with the same three datasets used for tailoring. The reported human-study population broadens from CS students to students spanning research fields including HCI, information science, education, and linguistics (§5.4; Appendix A.12).

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the same comparison methods: FS, SFT, DPO, their persona-tailored variants, and the LLaMA-405B teacher comparison. No evaluated comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: Persona-quality assessment and GPT-4o validation change from one to three annotators (§3.3; Appendix A.4). The user study reports eight participants, four per dataset, rather than ten in v1's main text; v1's appendix inconsistently lists five. Training settings remain unchanged. Both full and filtered Anthropic evaluations already existed, so their relocation introduces no new protocol.

E4.justification: The persona-validity sanity check and judge-reliability analysis gain multi-annotator evidence, with revised Figure 5 and expanded Appendices A.4/A.12. Existing verbosity controls, preference-flipping analysis, rejected-persona training ablations, system-prompt tests, and teacher–student comparisons remain substantially unchanged.

E5.justification: V2 adds Fleiss' kappa of 0.59 for judge-validation annotators and ordinal Krippendorff's alpha of 0.40 for persona applicability, plus agreement percentages for binary persona assessments. Single-run model reporting and Figure 6's 95% bootstrapped confidence-interval practice remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Human ratings change in Figures 5 and 6, and GPT-4o agreement changes from 86% to 90% under the expanded annotation setup. The user-study findings become more qualified for Anthropic HHH. Most apparent benchmark-score changes are relocations: v1 Table 15 matches v2 Table 2, while v1 Table 2 matches v2 Table 16.

T1.justification: The PI/PT definitions, training objectives, token-saliency formulation, and ΔPQ definition are retained. Neither version adds formal propositions or proofs. New discussion of multiple plausible personas explains evaluation choices without changing mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The principal claims about abductive persona inference, improved personalization, and challenging rejected-response personas remain. V2's conclusion adds a privacy-related benefit: inferred personas can support personalization without collecting potentially sensitive user data. Generalization to user-written personas was already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: V2 distinguishes strong BeaverTails user-study benefits from smaller Anthropic personalization gains with an answerability tradeoff. It adds single-example persona-inference limitations and resource tradeoffs, but removes explicit caveats about prompt sensitivity and testing only one teacher–student pairing. It also explains why persona inference lacks unique ground truth.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the inferred-persona output format and expands annotation documentation, including participant backgrounds, assignment across datasets, and the 144 authored personas. Appendix training hyperparameters, hardware, run budgets, and code/data access remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting persona rationalization, safeguards, privacy, and agreement measurement, including Joshi et al., Inan et al., Peng et al., and Fleiss et al. It further distinguishes its evaluation from prior personalization work and removes several application examples, while retaining the overall research positioning.

P1.justification: Prose is extensively revised across the abstract, introduction, evaluation rationale, method explanations, results discussion, and limitations. V2 also revises section headings, introduces numbered related-work subsections, and moves acknowledgments before limitations. This is a broad editorial revision despite substantial scientific continuity.

P2.justification: Full-set and filtered results exchange main-text and appendix placement, with Tables 15/16 reordered. Figure 6 moves and receives revised axes and caption; Table 1's caption expands, and Figure 2's section references are corrected. The overall visual organization and figure/table inventory remain.

improvement.justification: Multi-annotator validation and agreement statistics strengthen and clarify evidence previously relying on single annotators. The revised user-study discussion better acknowledges Anthropic HHH tradeoffs. These gains are limited by removed prompt-sensitivity/model-pairing caveats and remaining reporting inconsistencies: v2 Table 15 says full data although Appendix A.11 and the matched scores identify filtered results. The core benchmark evidence is largely unchanged.
